chapters.title: Structure and Bonding
chapters.summary: Reviews atoms, orbitals, and covalent bonding as the foundation for all of organic chemistry. Carbon is special because it forms four strong covalent bonds and bonds to itself in chains and rings; hybridization (sp3, sp2, sp) explains the tetrahedral, trigonal planar, and linear geometries of carbon, and skeletal structures are introduced as the working language for drawing molecules.
chapters.learner_can_do: Given a small molecule, draw its Lewis, line-bond, and skeletal structures, assign the hybridization of each carbon (and N, O, P, S), and predict bond angles and overall shape.
chapters.game_hook: Players build molecules atom by atom, snapping bonds onto hybrid orbitals whose geometry (109.5°, 120°, 180°) constrains where the next atom can attach; a molecule only 'locks' when every atom has a full valence shell.

sections.title: Why This Chapter?
sections.summary: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds; every living thing, medicine, and food is made of them. Historically 'organic' meant substances from living organisms, but by the mid-1800s it was clear the only distinguishing feature is carbon, which as a group 4A element shares four valence electrons and bonds to itself to make chains and rings.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: The Nucleus
sections.summary: An atom is a tiny dense positive nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons at about 10^-10 m. Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons; isotopes share Z but differ in A, and atomic weight is the abundance-weighted average mass in u (Da).

sections.game_hook: Assemble atoms from protons, neutrons, and electrons; adding neutrons changes the isotope (mass) but not the element's identity or chemistry.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: Orbitals
sections.summary: Electrons are described by wave functions (orbitals), regions where an electron spends 90–95% of its time. s orbitals are spherical, p orbitals are dumbbells with two lobes of opposite algebraic sign separated by a node, and d orbitals are mostly cloverleaf-shaped. Orbitals are grouped into shells of increasing size and energy holding 2, 8, and 18 electrons.
sections.learner_can_do: Recognize s, p, and d orbital shapes, identify nodes and lobe signs on a p orbital, and state how many electrons each shell holds.
sections.game_hook: Electron 'clouds' the player must fit into shells of limited capacity; p-orbital lobes carry +/- colors that matter later when orbitals overlap.

sections.title: Atomic Structure: Electron Configurations
sections.summary: Ground-state electron configurations follow three rules: fill lowest-energy orbitals first (Aufbau, with 4s between 3p and 3d), at most two electrons per orbital with opposite spins (Pauli), and spread electrons with parallel spins across equal-energy orbitals before pairing (Hund).

sections.game_hook: An orbital-filling puzzle: drop spin-up/spin-down electrons into energy-ordered boxes; the board rejects placements that break Aufbau, Pauli, or Hund.

sections.title: Development of Chemical Bonding Theory
sections.summary: Kekulé and Couper proposed tetravalent carbon that bonds into chains (and Kekulé, rings); van't Hoff and Le Bel added the tetrahedral 3D arrangement, drawn with solid, wedged, and dashed bonds. Atoms bond to reach a noble-gas octet: ionic bonds by electron transfer, covalent bonds by sharing. The number of bonds an atom forms equals the electrons it needs (H 1, C 4, N 3, O 2, halogens 1); leftover valence electrons are lone pairs. Lewis (electron-dot) and Kekulé (line-bond) structures represent molecules.
sections.learner_can_do: Predict how many bonds an atom forms from its group, draw electron-dot and line-bond structures (e.g., CH3Cl, PH3), and draw a tetrahedral carbon with wedge/dash bonds.
sections.game_hook: Atoms arrive with a fixed number of open 'bond sockets' set by their valence; players connect them into molecules where every atom reaches an octet, with lone pairs shown as unused sockets.

sections.title: Describing Chemical Bonds: Valence Bond Theory
sections.summary: In valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms when singly occupied orbitals on two atoms overlap and the paired electrons are attracted to both nuclei. Head-on overlap gives cylindrically symmetric sigma (σ) bonds. Forming H–H releases 436 kJ/mol (the bond strength); the bond length (74 pm for H2) is the internuclear distance at the energy minimum, balancing attraction against nuclear repulsion.

sections.game_hook: Pull two atoms together on an energy landscape: too far and nothing bonds, too close and they repel; the player finds the energy well that defines the bond length.

sections.title: sp3 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Methane
sections.summary: Methane's four identical tetrahedral C–H bonds are explained by Pauling's hybridization: one 2s and three 2p orbitals mix into four equivalent, unsymmetrical sp3 hybrids pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Their large lobe overlaps strongly, giving C–H bonds of 439 kJ/mol and 109 pm with 109.5° bond angles.
sections.learner_can_do: Explain why methane has four equivalent bonds and state the tetrahedral bond angle of an sp3 carbon.
sections.game_hook: Mix one s and three p orbitals in a 'hybridization forge' to produce four sp3 lobes that snap into a tetrahedron.

sections.title: sp2 Hybrid Orbitals and the Structure of Ethylene
sections.summary: A carbon double bond uses sp2 hybridization: one 2s plus two 2p orbitals give three planar sp2 hybrids at 120°, leaving one p orbital perpendicular. Two sp2 carbons form an sp2–sp2 σ bond plus a sideways p–p pi (π) bond. Ethylene is planar, with a shorter and stronger C=C (134 pm, 728 kJ/mol) than ethane's C–C, but less than twice as strong because π overlap is weaker. Carbonyl carbons such as in formaldehyde are also sp2.
sections.learner_can_do: Identify sp2 atoms in a molecule (alkenes, C=O), predict 120° angles, and explain the σ + π makeup of a double bond.
sections.game_hook: Two sp2 carbons can only form their π bond when their leftover p orbitals are parallel; players must align them, which locks the pieces flat.

sections.title: Describing Chemical Bonds: Molecular Orbital Theory
sections.summary: Molecular orbital theory combines atomic orbitals into molecular orbitals that belong to the whole molecule. Additive combination gives a lower-energy bonding MO concentrated between nuclei; subtractive combination gives a higher-energy antibonding MO with a node between nuclei. In H2 and in ethylene's π bond only the bonding MO is filled.
sections.learner_can_do: Sketch bonding and antibonding MOs for H2 or a C=C π bond, identify the node, and say which is occupied.
sections.game_hook: Combine two orbitals in phase (same color lobes) to drop energy and bond, or out of phase to create a node that pushes atoms apart.

sections.title: Drawing Chemical Structures
sections.summary: Condensed structures omit C–H and C–C single bonds (CH3CH2CH3, (CH3)2CH...). Skeletal structures go further: carbons sit at line ends and vertices, hydrogens on carbon are implied by carbon's valence of four, and heteroatoms are shown explicitly. Reading a skeletal structure means counting hydrogens at each vertex to get the molecular formula.

chapters.title: Polar Covalent Bonds; Acids and Bases
chapters.summary: Explains why molecules react by looking at how electrons are distributed: electronegativity makes bonds polar, polar bonds and lone pairs make molecules polar, formal charges track electron ownership, resonance spreads π and lone-pair electrons over several atoms, and acid–base behavior (Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis) follows from where electrons sit. Curved arrows are introduced as the notation for electron flow.
chapters.learner_can_do: Predict bond and molecular polarity, assign formal charges, draw valid resonance forms with curved arrows, and use pKa values to predict which way an acid–base reaction goes.

sections.title: Why This Chapter?
sections.summary: Understanding organic chemistry means knowing why and how reactions happen at the molecular level; bond polarity, acid–base behavior, and hydrogen bonding are the foundation for later reactions.

sections.title: Polar Covalent Bonds and Electronegativity
sections.summary: Most bonds are between ionic and covalent: polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally because of electronegativity (EN; F 4.0, O 3.5, N 3.0, C 2.5, H 2.1, Cs 0.7). EN differences under 0.5 are nonpolar, 0.5–2 polar, over 2 largely ionic. Partial charges are shown with δ+/δ− and crossed arrows, and electrostatic potential maps color electron-rich regions red and electron-poor blue. The inductive effect is electron shifting in σ bonds caused by nearby electronegative atoms (or electropositive metals).
sections.learner_can_do: Use electronegativity values to predict the direction of polarity of a bond (e.g., C–O, C–Li, C–Mg) and rank bonds from least to most polar.
sections.game_hook: A tug-of-war over the shared electron pair: stronger-EN atoms pull the electron cloud toward themselves, recoloring the bond red/blue like an electrostatic potential map.

sections.title: Polar Covalent Bonds and Dipole Moments
sections.summary: A molecule's polarity is the vector sum of its bond polarities and lone-pair contributions, measured as the dipole moment μ = Q × r in debyes. Molecules with electronegative atoms and lone pairs (H2O, CH3OH, NH3) have large dipoles; symmetric molecules (CO2, CH4, ethane, benzene) have zero because contributions cancel. Polar substances tend to dissolve in polar solvents like water.
sections.learner_can_do: Draw a molecule in 3D and decide whether it has a net dipole moment, and in which direction, from its symmetry, bond polarities, and lone pairs.
sections.game_hook: Add bond-dipole arrows as vectors; symmetric arrangements cancel to zero and the molecule stops responding to an electric field.

sections.title: Formal Charges
sections.summary: Formal charge is electron bookkeeping: valence electrons of the free atom minus electrons the bonded atom 'owns' (half the bonding electrons plus all nonbonding electrons). Atoms with unusual bond counts carry formal charges, e.g., S+ and O− in dimethyl sulfoxide. Table 2.2 summarizes common cases (C with 3 bonds can be 0, +1, or −1; N with 4 bonds is +1; O with 3 bonds is +1 and with 1 bond is −1).

sections.title: Rules for Resonance Forms
sections.summary: Five rules for resonance: (1) individual forms are imaginary and the hybrid is real; (2) forms differ only in placement of π or nonbonding electrons, with atoms and hybridization fixed, and curved arrows show electron (not atom) movement; (3) forms need not be equivalent, and the hybrid resembles the more stable one (e.g., negative charge on O in the acetone anion); (4) every form must obey normal valence and octet rules; (5) the hybrid is more stable than any single form, and more forms mean more stability.

sections.summary: H+ always moves from the stronger acid to the stronger base, so an acid–base reaction goes toward the weaker acid and weaker base. Comparing pKa values predicts whether a reaction proceeds (hydroxide deprotonates acetic acid, but not acetylene, pKa 25). Ka is found from pKa by antilog.

sections.title: Organic Acids and Organic Bases
sections.summary: Organic acids have a positively polarized H, either on O (methanol, acetic acid, whose conjugate bases put charge on O, and for acetate also resonance) or on C next to C=O (acetone, whose anion is resonance-stabilized with charge on O). Carboxylic acids exist as carboxylates at cellular pH 7.3. Organic bases have a lone pair that can take H+, most often nitrogen (amines); some compounds act as both. Amino acids exist mainly as zwitterions.
sections.learner_can_do: Identify the acidic hydrogens and basic sites in an organic molecule and explain the conjugate-base stabilization that makes it acidic.
sections.game_hook: Scan a molecule for blue (acidic) hydrogens and red (basic) lone pairs; plucking an H is easier when the leftover charge can hide on oxygen or spread by resonance.

sections.title: Acids and Bases: The Lewis Definition
sections.summary: Lewis acids accept an electron pair and Lewis bases donate one, forming a shared covalent bond. Lewis acids have a vacant low-energy orbital or can donate H+ (H+, Mg2+, BF3, AlCl3, TiCl4, FeCl3, ZnCl2, SnCl4); Lewis bases have lone pairs (H2O, alcohols, ethers, amines, carbonyl compounds). A curved arrow from the base's lone pair to the acid shows electron flow. Multi-site bases like acetic acid protonate where the product is most stable (the C=O oxygen, resonance-stabilized).

sections.game_hook: Lone pairs are hooks and empty orbitals are sockets; drawing a curved arrow from hook to socket forms the bond.

sections.title: Noncovalent Interactions between Molecules
sections.summary: Noncovalent (intermolecular, van der Waals) interactions include dipole–dipole forces between polar molecules (attractive when unlike ends meet), dispersion forces from fleeting temporary dipoles in all molecules, and hydrogen bonds between an H on O or N and a lone pair on another O or N. Hydrogen bonds keep water liquid, shape enzymes, and pair DNA strands. Hydrophilic substances (many –OH groups) dissolve in water; hydrophobic ones don't.
sections.learner_can_do: Identify which intermolecular force dominates in a substance and predict relative boiling points and water solubility (e.g., vitamin C hydrophilic vs. vitamin A hydrophobic).
sections.game_hook: Molecules stick together by visible tethers: weak flickering dispersion links, oriented dipole magnets, and strong O–H···O hydrogen bonds that decide whether a substance dissolves.

sections.title: Chemistry Matters—Alkaloids: From Cocaine to Dental Anesthetics
sections.summary: Alkaloids are naturally occurring basic amines; about half of today's drugs derive from natural amines (morphine, ephedrine, cocaine). The search for non-addictive analogs of cocaine led to the 'caine' anesthetics (procaine/Novocain, lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine), which share structural features with cocaine.

chapters.title: Organic Compounds: Alkanes and Their Stereochemistry
chapters.summary: Introduces functional groups, the reactive units that sort 195 million compounds into a few dozen predictable families, then uses alkanes to teach isomerism, alkyl groups, IUPAC naming, physical properties, and the first look at 3D shape: rotation about C–C single bonds and the energy cost of eclipsed and gauche conformations.
chapters.learner_can_do: Identify functional groups in a molecule, draw and name constitutional isomers and branched alkanes by IUPAC rules, and draw Newman projections to rank alkane conformations by strain energy.
chapters.game_hook: Players name molecules by tracing the longest chain through a branching maze, and twist C–C bonds on a Newman-projection dial to find energy valleys (staggered, anti) and avoid peaks (eclipsed).

sections.title: Why This Chapter?
sections.summary: Alkanes are simple and unreactive but are the vehicle for introducing naming and the three-dimensional aspects of molecules. Organic compounds fall into families with similar behavior, starting with alkanes.

sections.title: Functional Groups
sections.summary: A functional group is a group of atoms with characteristic chemical behavior that is nearly the same in every molecule containing it; e.g., ethylene and menthene both add Br2 across their C=C. Table 3.1 lists families: C–C multiple bonds (alkenes, alkynes, arenes); carbon singly bonded to an electronegative atom (alkyl halides, alcohols, ethers, phosphates, amines, thiols, sulfides, disulfides), all with δ+ carbon; and carbonyl groups (aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, thioesters, amides, acid chlorides, anhydrides), all with δ+ carbonyl carbon and δ− oxygen.
sections.learner_can_do: Locate and name every functional group in a given molecule (e.g., arecoline, statins) and propose simple structures containing a specified functional group.
sections.game_hook: Functional groups are 'power-ups' that define how a molecule behaves; a huge molecule and a tiny one with the same group react the same way in a demonstration.

sections.title: Alkanes and Alkane Isomers
sections.summary: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, CnH2n+2, built from sp3 carbons joined by single bonds. From C4 on, carbons can be arranged in different ways: straight-chain (normal) vs. branched alkanes. Isomers share a formula but differ in structure; constitutional isomers differ in connectivity (butane vs. isobutane, ethanol vs. dimethyl ether, propylamine vs. isopropylamine). Isomer counts explode with size (C30H62 has over 4 billion). The first ten straight-chain alkane names should be memorized.

sections.title: Alkyl Groups
sections.summary: Removing an H from an alkane gives an alkyl group (methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl...; -ane becomes -yl). Removing an internal H gives branched groups: isopropyl, sec-butyl, isobutyl, tert-butyl. Carbons are primary, secondary, tertiary, or quaternary by how many other carbons they bond to, and hydrogens are classified by their carbon. R stands for the rest of the molecule.

sections.title: Naming Alkanes
sections.summary: IUPAC names have a parent, prefixes, locants, and a suffix. Steps: (1) find the longest continuous chain (turning corners; with ties, the more branched one); (2) number from the end nearer the first branch (ties go to the second branch); (3) number each substituent; (4) write one word with alphabetized substituents, di-/tri- multipliers ignored for alphabetizing; (5) name complex branched substituents as their own units in parentheses. Common names isopropyl, isobutyl, sec-butyl, and tert-butyl are allowed.

chapters.title: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
chapters.summary: Rings restrict rotation, which creates cis–trans stereoisomers and ring strain. The chapter measures strain from heats of combustion, explains why only cyclohexane is strain-free (the chair conformation), and develops conformational analysis: axial vs. equatorial positions, ring-flips, 1,3-diaxial interactions, and how to pick the more stable chair for substituted and fused rings.
chapters.learner_can_do: Name substituted cycloalkanes with cis/trans prefixes, draw both chair conformations of a substituted cyclohexane, label each group axial or equatorial, and use 1,3-diaxial strain values to decide which chair is favored and by how much.
chapters.game_hook: A cyclohexane chair the player can ring-flip; every flip swaps axial and equatorial seats, and bulky groups take a strain penalty when forced into axial seats, so the player must seat substituents to minimize strain.

sections.summary: Cycloalkanes (alicyclic compounds) have formula CnH2n and are drawn as polygons. Naming: if the ring has at least as many carbons as the largest substituent, name as an alkyl-substituted cycloalkane, otherwise as a cycloalkyl-substituted alkane. sections.title: Cis–Trans Isomerism in Cycloalkanes
sections.summary: Rings are much less flexible than chains (cyclopropane is rigid and planar), so a ring has a top and a bottom face. sections.title: Stability of Cycloalkanes: Ring Strain
sections.summary: Baeyer proposed angle strain from flat-ring geometry. Measuring heats of combustion per CH2 shows cyclopropane and cyclobutane are strained, cyclopentane is more strained than predicted, cyclohexane is strain-free, and rings of 14+ are strain-free. Baeyer was wrong because rings pucker. Total strain combines angle strain, torsional strain (eclipsing), and steric strain (atoms too close).

sections.title: Axial and Equatorial Bonds in Cyclohexane
sections.summary: Each chair carbon has one axial position (parallel to the ring axis) and one equatorial position (around the ring's equator), alternating up and down around the ring. Cis/trans depends only on which face a group is on, not on axial/equatorial. A ring-flip (barrier about 45 kJ/mol, fast at room temperature) converts every axial position to equatorial and vice versa, so monosubstituted cyclohexanes exist as one compound.

chapters.title: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
chapters.summary: Molecular handedness: a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups makes a molecule chiral, giving non-superimposable mirror-image enantiomers that differ only in how they rotate plane-polarized light and in how they interact with other chiral things such as enzymes. The chapter develops R/S naming by the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules, diastereomers, meso compounds, racemates and their resolution, a map of all isomer types, and prochirality (Re/Si faces, pro-R/pro-S groups).
chapters.learner_can_do: Find chirality centers, assign R or S by CIP ranking, classify pairs of stereoisomers as enantiomers, diastereomers, or identical (meso), and identify Re/Si faces and pro-R/pro-S hydrogens.
chapters.game_hook: Mirror-world puzzles: the player rotates 3D molecules trying to superimpose them on their reflections, ranks groups by CIP priority to read the steering-wheel direction (R/S), and fits the correct-handed key into a chiral enzyme lock.

sections.title: Enantiomers and the Tetrahedral Carbon
sections.summary: CH3X and CH2XY are identical to their mirror images, but CHXYZ (four different groups) is not, just as left and right hands aren't superimposable. Non-superimposable mirror-image stereoisomers are enantiomers; lactic acid (−H, −OH, −CH3, −CO2H on one carbon) exists as (+) and (−) forms, and no orientation makes them coincide.
sections.learner_can_do: Decide whether a tetrahedral carbon bears four different groups and draw the two enantiomers with wedges and dashes (e.g., lactic acid, alanine).
sections.game_hook: Try to overlay a molecule on its mirror image by rotating it; with four different groups, two always end up mismatched.

sections.title: The Reason for Handedness in Molecules: Chirality
sections.summary: A molecule not identical to its mirror image is chiral; a molecule with a plane of symmetry in any conformation is achiral (propanoic acid vs. lactic acid). The usual cause is a chirality center: a tetrahedral carbon with four different groups, where the difference may be several atoms away (5-bromodecane). Ring examples: methylcyclohexane is achiral, 2-methylcyclohexanone is chiral. CH2, CH3, and sp2/sp carbons can't be chirality centers.
sections.learner_can_do: Identify all chirality centers in a molecule and decide whether the whole molecule is chiral by looking for a symmetry plane.
sections.game_hook: Slice molecules with a mirror plane tool; if no slice makes the halves match, the molecule is chiral and its chirality centers glow.

sections.title: Optical Activity
sections.summary: Biot found that solutions of some organic compounds rotate plane-polarized light (optical activity), measured with a polarimeter. Clockwise rotation is dextrorotatory (+), counterclockwise levorotatory (−). Observed rotation scales with concentration and pathlength, so specific rotation [α]D = α / (l × c) at the 589.6 nm sodium D line (l in dm, c in g/cm3) is a physical constant; enantiomers have equal and opposite values (±3.82 for lactic acid).
sections.learner_can_do: Compute observed rotation or specific rotation from concentration and pathlength (e.g., cocaine, coniine).
sections.game_hook: A polarimeter puzzle: shine polarized light through sample tubes and turn the analyzer until light passes; longer tubes or stronger solutions twist it more.

sections.title: Pasteur’s Discovery of Enantiomers
sections.summary: In 1848 Pasteur crystallized sodium ammonium tartrate and hand-sorted two mirror-image crystal forms whose solutions rotated light equally in opposite directions. He proposed molecular asymmetry decades before the tetrahedral carbon. Enantiomers (optical isomers) share physical properties except the direction of optical rotation.

sections.title: Sequence Rules for Specifying Configuration
sections.summary: Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules rank groups on a chirality center: (1) by atomic number of the directly attached atom (heavier isotope higher); (2) if tied, compare the next atoms out until a difference; (3) multiple bonds count as duplicated single-bonded atoms. With the lowest-ranked group pointing away, a clockwise 1→2→3 path is R, counterclockwise is S. R/S has no simple relation to the sign of optical rotation ((S)-glyceraldehyde is (−), (S)-alanine is (+)); absolute configuration was settled by X-ray in 1951.
sections.learner_can_do: Rank four substituents by CIP rules and assign R or S to a chirality center drawn in any orientation; draw a specified enantiomer such as (R)-2-chlorobutane.
sections.game_hook: A steering-wheel challenge: rank the groups, push the lowest one to the back, and turn the wheel 1→2→3—right turn is R, left turn is S.

sections.title: Diastereomers
sections.summary: A molecule with n chirality centers has up to 2^n stereoisomers. Threonine (two centers) has four: two enantiomer pairs (2R,3R/2S,3S and 2R,3S/2S,3R). Stereoisomers that aren't mirror images are diastereomers—opposite at some centers, the same at others. Epimers are diastereomers differing at only one center (cholestanol and coprostanol at C5). Usually only one stereoisomer occurs in nature (2S,3R-threonine).

sections.title: Chirality in Nature and Chiral Environments
sections.summary: Enantiomers have identical physical properties but often different biological effects, because biological receptors are chiral: only one enantiomer fits, like a hand in the matching glove (e.g., (S)-fluoxetine prevents migraine). A chiral environment also makes the two identical groups of a prochiral molecule distinguishable, which is how enzymes select pro-R vs. pro-S hydrogens, much as your hand makes one side of a symmetric mug the drinking side.
sections.learner_can_do: Explain with a three-point-binding model why a chiral receptor distinguishes enantiomers and the two faces or groups of a prochiral substrate.
sections.game_hook: A three-pocket enzyme lock: only one enantiomer seats all three groups, and a prochiral substrate seats with only one of its twin groups exposed for reaction.

chapters.title: An Overview of Organic Reactions
chapters.summary: A framework for every reaction in the book: four reaction types (addition, elimination, substitution, rearrangement), two main mechanism types (polar, driven by nucleophile–electrophile attraction and drawn with full curved arrows; radical, with odd electrons and fishhook arrows), and the energy language for describing reactions—Keq and ΔG° for how far, ΔG‡ for how fast, bond dissociation energies, energy diagrams with transition states and intermediates—plus how enzyme-catalyzed biological reactions differ from lab reactions.

chapters.game_hook: Reactions as journeys over an energy landscape: the player fires electron-pair arrows from nucleophilic sources to electrophilic sinks to move molecules through transition-state passes and intermediate valleys, needing enough activation energy to clear each pass.

sections.title: Why This Chapter?
sections.summary: All reactions, in the lab or in living cells, follow the same rules; organic chemistry is unified by a few broad themes, so understanding why and how reactions occur minimizes memorization.

sections.title: How Organic Reactions Occur: Mechanisms
sections.summary: A reaction mechanism describes which bonds break and form, in what order, and how fast each step is. Bonds break heterolytically (both electrons to one fragment, full-headed curved arrow) or homolytically (one electron each, fishhook arrow), and form the same two ways. Polar reactions use unsymmetrical bond changes and are most common; radical reactions use symmetrical changes and involve species with an unpaired electron; pericyclic reactions are a third, rarer type.

sections.title: Polar Reactions
sections.summary: Polar reactions happen because electron-rich sites attract electron-poor ones. Carbon bonded to more electronegative atoms is δ+, and bonded to metals is δ− (Table 6.1). Protonation by acid makes a carbon more electron-poor, and polarizability lets C–S and C–I bonds react as if polar. A nucleophile donates an electron pair (NH3, H2O, HO−, Cl−); an electrophile accepts one (H+ donors, alkyl halides, carbonyl compounds). Nucleophiles are Lewis bases and electrophiles are Lewis acids; neutral molecules can act as either.

sections.title: Describing a Reaction: Equilibria, Rates, and Energy Changes
sections.summary: The equilibrium constant Keq tells which side is favored (Keq > 10^3 means essentially complete). Keq relates to the standard free-energy change by ΔG° = −RT ln Keq; negative ΔG° is exergonic, positive is endergonic. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: ΔH (heat of reaction) reflects bond strengths (exothermic if negative), and ΔS reflects randomness (positive for eliminations, negative for additions). Ethylene + HBr has Keq ≈ 7.1 × 10^7 and ΔG° = −44.8 kJ/mol. Equilibria say how much, not how fast.

sections.title: Describing a Reaction: Energy Diagrams and Transition States
sections.summary: Energy diagrams plot energy against the reaction coordinate. The transition state is the highest-energy structure in a step, an unisolable activated complex with bonds partly broken and formed. Activation energy ΔG‡ (reactants to transition state) sets the rate; ΔG° (reactants to products) sets the equilibrium. Typical organic ΔG‡ values are 40–150 kJ/mol; below about 80 kJ/mol reactions run at room temperature. Ethylene + HBr's first step has ΔG‡ ≈ 140 kJ/mol and is endergonic.

sections.title: Describing a Reaction: Intermediates
sections.summary: A reaction intermediate, like the carbocation in HBr addition, sits in an energy minimum between two transition states; it is more stable than its neighboring transition states but usually too unstable to isolate. Multistep diagrams join each step; the overall rate is set by the highest transition state relative to reactants, and overall ΔG° is reactants versus final products. Enzymes split biological reactions into many small steps with low barriers and small energy changes.

chapters.title: Alkenes: Structure and Reactivity
chapters.summary: Alkenes: how they are made industrially, how to count rings and π bonds from a formula (degree of unsaturation), how to name them and specify double-bond geometry (cis/trans and E/Z), why more substituted and trans alkenes are more stable, and their signature reaction—electrophilic addition of HX through carbocation intermediates. Markovnikov's rule follows from carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1° > methyl) via the Hammond postulate, and carbocation rearrangements (hydride and alkyl shifts) are key evidence for the mechanism.
chapters.learner_can_do: Calculate degree of unsaturation, name alkenes with E/Z, rank alkene and carbocation stabilities, and predict the Markovnikov product of HX addition, including any hydride or alkyl shift.
chapters.game_hook: HX addition as a branching path: the player chooses which alkene carbon the proton lands on, sees the resulting carbocation's stability bar, and can trigger hydride or methyl shifts to slide the positive charge to a more substituted carbon before the halide arrives.

sections.title: Industrial Preparation and Use of Alkenes
sections.summary: Ethylene and propylene are the most important industrial organic chemicals (hundreds of millions of tons per year), feeding polyethylene, polypropylene, ethylene glycol, and more. They're made by steam cracking C2–C8 alkanes at up to 900 °C, a radical process that is endothermic but driven by a large positive entropy change at high temperature (TΔS° > ΔH°).

sections.title: Calculating the Degree of Unsaturation
sections.summary: Each ring or π bond removes two hydrogens from the saturated formula CnH2n+2, so the degree of unsaturation (rings + multiple bonds) can be computed from a molecular formula: add halogens to hydrogens, ignore oxygens, and subtract nitrogens from hydrogens. C6H10 has two degrees: two double bonds, a ring plus a double bond, two rings, or a triple bond.

sections.title: Naming Alkenes
sections.summary: Alkenes are named with -ene: find the longest chain containing the C=C, number from the end nearer the double bond (or nearer the first branch if tied), and give the first alkene carbon's locant; use -diene, -triene for several. Cycloalkenes put the double bond at C1–C2. Common names (ethylene, propylene, isobutylene, isoprene) and groups (methylene =CH2, vinyl, allyl) are accepted. Post-1993 IUPAC names put the locant before -ene (but-2-ene).

sections.title: Stability of Alkenes
sections.summary: Trans alkenes are more stable than cis (trans-2-butene by 2.8 kJ/mol, 76:24 at equilibrium) because of steric strain between cis substituents. Heats of hydrogenation measure relative stability: more substituted alkenes release less heat (ethylene −136, tetrasubstituted −110 kJ/mol), so stability increases with substitution. Reasons: hyperconjugation between the π orbital and neighboring C–H σ bonds, and stronger sp2–sp3 bonds.

sections.title: Electrophilic Addition Reactions of Alkenes
sections.summary: Alkenes react as nucleophiles in electrophilic addition: the π electrons attack H of HX to form a carbocation (slow step, larger ΔG‡), then the halide adds to the cation (fast step). The overall reaction is exergonic with two transition states and a carbocation intermediate. HCl, HBr, HI (from KI and H3PO4), and H2O (with acid catalyst) all add. Reactions can be written with reagents above the arrow, and biological reactions with abbreviated coenzymes.

sections.title: Carbocation Structure and Stability
sections.summary: Carbocations are planar sp2 carbons with an empty p orbital. Stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, shown by alkyl halide dissociation enthalpies. Alkyl groups stabilize the cation through inductive electron donation and through hyperconjugation of neighboring C–H σ bonds aligned with the empty p orbital.

sections.game_hook: Neighboring alkyl groups lend electron density to fill an empty orbital; more neighbors means a steadier, longer-lived cation.

sections.title: The Hammond Postulate
sections.summary: The Hammond postulate links stability to rate: a transition state resembles the nearest stable species, so for an endergonic step it resembles the product, and for an exergonic step the reactant. Alkene protonation is endergonic, so its transition state resembles the carbocation, and whatever stabilizes the cation also lowers the barrier. That is why more stable carbocations form faster.
sections.learner_can_do: Use the Hammond postulate to predict which of two alkenes forms a carbocation faster and whether a step's transition state looks like reactant or product.
sections.game_hook: Lowering the valley (intermediate) also lowers the nearby pass (transition state) in an energy-landscape editor.

sections.title: Evidence for the Mechanism of Electrophilic Additions: Carbocation Rearrangements
sections.summary: Mechanisms can't be proven, only shown consistent with the facts. Whitmore found rearranged products in HX additions (3-methyl-1-butene gives 2-chloro-2-methylbutane), explained by carbocation intermediates that rearrange to more stable ions via a hydride shift (H with its electron pair) or an alkyl shift (e.g., methyl from 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene). Such shifts are important in steroid biosynthesis (cholesterol).

sections.title: Chemistry Matters—Bioprospecting: Hunting for Natural Products
sections.summary: Natural products are small secondary metabolites (over 300,000 estimated), such as alkaloids, antibiotics, and immunosuppressants like rapamycin from an Easter Island soil bacterium. chapters.title: Alkenes: Reactions and Synthesis
chapters.summary: The alkene reaction toolkit. Alkenes are made by eliminations (dehydrohalogenation, dehydration) and undergo many additions, each with its own regiochemistry and stereochemistry: X2 (anti, via halonium ion), HOX halohydrins (Markovnikov, anti), oxymercuration (Markovnikov hydration), hydroboration (non-Markovnikov, syn), catalytic hydrogenation (syn), epoxidation and OsO4 hydroxylation (syn), epoxide hydrolysis (anti), oxidative cleavage (O3, KMnO4, HIO4), carbene cyclopropanation, and radical chain-growth polymerization. The chapter closes on the stereochemistry of new chirality centers: achiral reactants give racemates, chiral reactants give unequal diastereomers.
chapters.learner_can_do: Choose the reagent that converts an alkene into a target product with the right regiochemistry (Markovnikov vs. non-Markovnikov) and stereochemistry (syn vs. anti), and work backward from products (including ozonolysis fragments) to the starting alkene.
chapters.game_hook: A reagent spell-book: each alkene reagent is a card with a visible signature (which carbon gets which group, same face vs. opposite faces); the player sequences cards to synthesize target molecules, and wrong-face or wrong-carbon additions produce the wrong stereoisomer.

sections.title: Reduction of Alkenes: Hydrogenation
sections.summary: H2 with Pd/C or PtO2 (Adams' catalyst) reduces alkenes to alkanes. In organic chemistry, reduction means carbon gains electron density (bonds to H, or loses bonds to O/N/X). Hydrogenation is heterogeneous, happens on the catalyst surface, adds both H syn, and approaches from the less hindered face (α-pinene). Alkenes are reduced selectively over C=O, esters, nitriles, and aromatic rings. Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils makes trans fats. Biological reductions use NADPH hydride addition next to a carbonyl, then protonation.

sections.summary: Carbenes (R2C:) are neutral, divalent, six-electron carbons that act as electrophiles and add to alkenes in one step to make cyclopropanes. Dichlorocarbene forms from CHCl3 and KOH (deprotonation, then loss of Cl−); like a carbocation, it is sp2 with a vacant p orbital, plus a lone pair. sections.title: Radical Additions to Alkenes: Chain-Growth Polymers
sections.summary: Polymers are built from repeating monomers. Chain-growth polymers like polyethylene (up to 200,000 units) form by radical chain reactions: initiation (benzoyl peroxide gives phenyl radicals that add to ethylene), propagation (radical adds to monomer after monomer), and termination (two radicals combine). Vinyl monomers polymerize with substituents on alternating carbons through the more substituted radical (polypropylene, polystyrene, PVC, Teflon, Plexiglas; Table 8.1).

chapters.title: Alkynes: An Introduction to Organic Synthesis
chapters.summary: Alkynes (C≡C, sp carbons, linear) are prepared by double elimination of HX from vicinal dihalides and by alkylation of acetylide anions. They undergo alkene-like electrophilic additions (HX, X2), hydration to ketones via enol tautomers (Hg2+ for Markovnikov methyl ketones, disiamylborane hydroboration for aldehydes), reduction (Pd to alkanes, Lindlar to cis alkenes, Li/NH3 to trans alkenes), and oxidative cleavage. Terminal alkynes are unusually acidic (pKa 25) because of 50% s character. The chapter uses these reactions to introduce retrosynthetic planning of multistep syntheses.
chapters.learner_can_do: Predict products of alkyne reactions, choose Lindlar vs. Li/NH3 for cis vs. trans alkenes, build carbon chains by acetylide alkylation with primary halides, and plan a multistep synthesis by working backward from the target.
chapters.game_hook: A retrosynthesis map: the player starts at the target molecule and walks backward one known reaction at a time to reach the allowed starting materials, chaining acetylide alkylations to grow carbon chains and choosing the right reduction to set cis or trans geometry.

sections.title: Naming Alkynes
sections.summary: Alkynes use the suffix -yne, numbered from the end nearer the triple bond. Multiple triple bonds give diynes, triynes; compounds with both give enynes, numbered from the end nearer the first multiple bond, with double bonds getting lower numbers when there's a choice. Alkynyl substituents exist too.

sections.title: Hydration of Alkynes
sections.summary: HgSO4-catalyzed hydration (aqueous H2SO4) follows Markovnikov regiochemistry and gives an enol that immediately tautomerizes to a ketone (keto–enol tautomerism; tautomers interconvert by moving a hydrogen). sections.title: An Introduction to Organic Synthesis
sections.summary: Planning a synthesis requires knowing each reaction's uses and limits and making each step change only what's intended. The key strategy is retrosynthetic: start at the product and ask what its immediate precursor was, stepping back to the starting material. Worked examples: cis-2-hexene from 1-pentyne (alkylate with CH3I, then Lindlar); 2-bromopentane from acetylene (alkylate, Lindlar, Markovnikov HBr); 5-methyl-1-hexanol (alkylate, Lindlar, hydroboration–oxidation).

chapters.title: Organohalides
chapters.summary: Organohalides: naming haloalkanes, the polar and electrophilic C–X bond, and ways to make alkyl halides—radical halogenation of alkanes (mixtures, selectivity from radical stability), allylic bromination with NBS (via resonance-stabilized allyl radicals), and conversion of alcohols (HX for tertiary; SOCl2, PBr3, HF–pyridine for primary/secondary). Alkyl halides become carbon nucleophiles as Grignard reagents and organolithiums, and form C–C bonds in Gilman (R2CuLi) and Suzuki–Miyaura couplings. The chapter defines organic oxidation and reduction by counting bonds to heteroatoms versus hydrogen.
chapters.learner_can_do: Name alkyl halides, predict radical and allylic halogenation products and ratios, choose reagents to turn alcohols into alkyl halides, use organometallic couplings to join carbon fragments, and rank compounds by oxidation level.
chapters.game_hook: A radical-hunt arena where Br· and Cl· radicals pick off the weakest C–H bonds first (allylic > 3° > 2° > 1°), and an organometallic forge that flips electrophilic C–X carbons into nucleophilic C–Mg or C–Cu carbons that can bond to other fragments.

sections.title: Names and Structures of Alkyl Halides
sections.summary: Haloalkanes are named with the halogen as a substituent: the longest chain (containing any multiple bond) is the parent, numbered from the end nearer the first substituent of any kind; different halogens are listed alphabetically, and ties go to alphabetical precedence. sections.title: Stability of the Allyl Radical: Resonance Revisited
sections.summary: The allyl radical is sp2 and electronically symmetric, so its unpaired electron is delocalized over both end carbons (two resonance forms; spin density shared equally), making it extra stable. As a result, allylic bromination of an unsymmetrical alkene can give mixtures (1-octene gives 3-bromo-1-octene and 1-bromo-2-octene, favoring reaction at the less hindered end). Allylic bromides can be dehydrohalogenated to dienes.

sections.title: Reactions of Alkyl Halides: Grignard Reagents
sections.summary: Alkyl, vinylic, and aryl halides (Cl, Br, I) react with Mg in ether or THF to give Grignard reagents, RMgX—organometallic compounds with a polarized C–Mg bond that makes carbon nucleophilic and strongly basic. A Grignard is formally a carbanion salt of a very weak carbon acid (pKa 44–60), so water destroys it (R–MgX + H2O gives R–H).

sections.title: Organometallic Coupling Reactions
sections.summary: Alkyl halides plus lithium give alkyllithiums (RLi); with CuI they form Gilman reagents (R2CuLi), which couple with alkyl, vinylic, and aryl chlorides, bromides, and iodides to form new C–C bonds (e.g., lithium dimethylcopper + 1-iododecane gives undecane; commercial muscalure synthesis). The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction couples aryl or vinyl boronic acids with aryl or vinyl halides using base and a catalytic palladium cycle, making biaryls such as the drug valsartan.

sections.title: Oxidation and Reduction in Organic Chemistry
sections.summary: Organic oxidation is loss of electron density at carbon (forming C–O, C–N, C–X bonds or breaking C–H); reduction is the reverse. Methane chlorination is an oxidation; converting an alkyl halide to an alkane through a Grignard is a reduction; HBr addition to an alkene is neither. Compounds with the same number of carbons can be ranked by (C–O + C–N + C–X bonds) minus C–H bonds, from alkanes (lowest) to CO2 (highest).

chapters.title: Reactions of Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitutions and Eliminations
chapters.summary: The two great competing reactions of alkyl halides with nucleophiles/bases: substitution and elimination. SN2 is one-step backside attack with inversion and second-order kinetics, fastest for methyl/primary substrates, strong nucleophiles, good leaving groups, and polar aprotic solvents. SN1 goes through a carbocation (first-order, mostly racemization), favored by tertiary/allylic/benzylic substrates and polar protic solvents. Eliminations follow Zaitsev's rule and occur as E2 (one step, anti periplanar, deuterium isotope effect, trans-diaxial in cyclohexanes), E1 (carbocation, competes with SN1), or E1cB (carbanion next to a carbonyl, common in biology). Biological versions use diphosphate leaving groups and SAM methylations.
chapters.learner_can_do: Given a substrate, nucleophile/base, leaving group, and solvent, predict whether SN1, SN2, E1, E2, or E1cB dominates and draw the product with correct stereochemistry (inversion, racemization, Zaitsev or anti-periplanar alkene).
chapters.game_hook: A reaction-arena strategy game: the player tunes four dials (substrate bulk, nucleophile/base strength, leaving group, solvent) and watches the substrate take one of five mechanistic paths—backside SN2 umbrella flip, carbocation SN1/E1, concerted anti-periplanar E2, or carbanion E1cB—with the product's stereochemistry as the score.

sections.title: Characteristics of the SN2 Reaction
sections.summary: SN2 rate depends on ΔG‡. Substrate: steric hindrance slows attack, so methyl > primary > secondary >> tertiary (no SN2); neopentyl is very slow, and vinylic/aryl halides don't react. Nucleophile: rates span 10^5 (Table 11.1); nucleophilicity parallels basicity for the same atom, increases down a group (HS− > HO−, I− > Br− > Cl−), and anions beat neutrals. Leaving group: weak bases leave best (tosylate, I−, Br−, Cl−); F−, HO−, RO−, H2N− don't, so alcohols must be activated (tosylates, SOCl2, PBr3), though strained epoxides open. Solvent: protic solvents cage and slow nucleophiles; polar aprotic solvents (CH3CN, DMF, DMSO, HMPA) speed SN2 enormously.

sections.title: The SN1 Reaction
sections.summary: Tertiary halides react with water a million times faster than CH3Br, with rate = k[RX] only (first-order). The SN1 mechanism (unimolecular): slow, rate-limiting dissociation to a planar carbocation, then fast capture by the nucleophile. Because the cation is achiral, an enantiopure substrate gives mostly racemic product, usually with a small excess of inversion because the departing anion briefly shields one face as an ion pair (Winstein).

sections.title: Characteristics of the SN1 Reaction
sections.summary: By the Hammond postulate, whatever stabilizes the carbocation speeds SN1. Substrate: 3° > 2° and resonance-stabilized allylic and benzylic cations (a primary allylic/benzylic cation is about as stable as a secondary alkyl one). Leaving group: same order as SN2; under acid, protonated alcohols lose neutral water, which is why HX converts tertiary alcohols to halides. Nucleophile: no effect on rate (neutral ones work fine) but should be nonbasic to avoid elimination. Solvent: polar protic solvents stabilize the cation and transition state (water is 10^5 faster than ethanol).

sections.title: Biological Substitution Reactions
sections.summary: Biological substitutions usually use organodiphosphates, with diphosphate (PPi), aided by Mg2+, as the biological equivalent of a halide leaving group. sections.title: Elimination Reactions: Zaitsev’s Rule
sections.summary: A nucleophile/base can instead remove a neighboring H and eliminate HX. sections.title: The E2 Reaction and the Deuterium Isotope Effect
sections.summary: E2 (bimolecular) occurs with strong bases (HO−, RO−) in one step with rate = k[RX][Base]. A deuterium isotope effect (C–H breaks 7.11× faster than C–D) shows C–H breaks in the rate-limiting step. E2 requires periplanar geometry (H, two C's, and X in one plane), strongly preferring anti periplanar (staggered) over syn periplanar (eclipsed), so stereochemistry is specific: meso-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane gives only the E alkene.

sections.title: The E1 and E1cB Reactions
sections.summary: E1 (unimolecular) shares SN1's rate-limiting carbocation formation, then loses a proton; SN1 and E1 compete under protic, nonbasic conditions (2-chloro-2-methylpropane in 80% ethanol gives 64:36 alcohol:alkene). E1 shows first-order kinetics, no deuterium isotope effect, no geometric requirement, and gives Zaitsev products (menthyl chloride gives mainly 3-menthene under E1). E1cB removes the proton first to form a carbanion, then expels the leaving group; it's favored for poor leaving groups like –OH two carbons from a carbonyl, which acidifies the adjacent H.

sections.title: A Summary of Reactivity: SN1, SN2, E1, E1cB, and E2
sections.summary: Rules of thumb: primary halides give SN2 with good nucleophiles, E2 with strong hindered bases, E1cB if the leaving group is β to a carbonyl. Secondary halides give SN2 with weakly basic nucleophiles in polar aprotic solvents, E2 with strong bases, and (if allylic/benzylic) SN1/E1 with weak nucleophiles in protic solvents. Tertiary halides give E2 with bases and SN1+E1 under neutral conditions (ethanol or water).
sections.learner_can_do: Classify any reaction as SN1, SN2, E1, E1cB, or E2 from its conditions and predict the product.

chapters.title: Structure Determination: Mass Spectrometry and Infrared Spectroscopy
chapters.summary: How chemists determine structure. Mass spectrometry ionizes molecules (electron impact, or soft ESI/MALDI for biomolecules), sorts ions by m/z, and gives molecular weight, exact formulas (high resolution), isotope patterns (Cl 3:1, Br 1:1 at M and M+2), the nitrogen rule, and fragmentation clues (α cleavage, dehydration, McLafferty rearrangement). Infrared spectroscopy measures which vibrational frequencies a molecule absorbs; characteristic bands (O–H, N–H, C–H, C≡C, C=O, C=C, fingerprint region) identify functional groups.
chapters.learner_can_do: Read a mass spectrum to find M+, the base peak, likely formula, halogen isotope patterns, and fragment losses, and read an IR spectrum to identify which functional groups are present (and absent).
chapters.game_hook: A detective lab: the player fires a mystery molecule through a mass spectrometer to get its weight and fragment 'debris', then shines IR light to see which bond-springs ring, and must name the culprit structure consistent with all the evidence.

sections.title: Why This Chapter?
sections.summary: Determining structures of new molecules is central to chemistry. Four techniques are covered across chapters: MS (size and formula), IR (functional groups), UV (conjugated π systems), and NMR (carbon–hydrogen framework).

sections.title: Mass Spectrometry of Small Molecules: Magnetic-Sector Instruments
sections.summary: Mass spectrometers have an ionization source, a mass analyzer, and a detector. In electron-impact magnetic-sector instruments, ~70 eV electrons knock out an electron to make a cation radical, which often fragments; a magnetic field sorts charged fragments by m/z (usually z = 1). Quadrupole analyzers pass only one m/z at a time. Spectra plot relative abundance vs. m/z; the tallest peak is the base peak and the unfragmented ion is the molecular ion (parent peak, M+). Propane shows M+ = 44 and base peak 29.
sections.learner_can_do: Identify the molecular ion and base peak in a mass spectrum and explain how ions are formed and sorted.
sections.game_hook: Molecules shot through a curved magnetic track: lighter fragments bend more, heavier ones less, and each lands on its own detector slot.

sections.title: Interpreting Mass Spectra
sections.summary: MS gives molecular weight (hexane 86, 1-hexene 84, 1-hexyne 82), and high-resolution (double-focusing) instruments give exact masses to ~0.0005 amu that distinguish formulas (C5H12 72.0939 vs. C4H8O 72.0575). Some compounds (2,2-dimethylpropane) show no M+. Small M+1 peaks arise from 13C (1.10%) and 2H. Spectra act as fingerprints, and fragments keep the charge on the more stable cation (tert-butyl, m/z 57). Hexane shows losses of CH3, C2H5, C3H7, C4H9 (m/z 71, 57, 43, 29); methylcyclohexane and ethylcyclopentane are told apart by loss of 15 vs. 29.
sections.learner_can_do: Propose molecular formulas from M+ or exact mass, and explain major fragment peaks as losses of alkyl radicals.
sections.game_hook: Subtract each fragment's mass from the parent to reveal which piece broke off, then reassemble the molecule from its debris.

sections.title: Mass Spectrometry of Some Common Functional Groups
sections.summary: Functional-group fragmentations: alcohols undergo α cleavage (C–C next to OH breaks, giving an oxygen-stabilized cation) and dehydration (loss of 18). The nitrogen rule: an odd number of nitrogens gives an odd M+. Amines undergo α cleavage (triethylamine base peak 86). Chlorine gives M and M+2 in a 3:1 ratio and bromine nearly 1:1. Ketones and aldehydes show α cleavage to acyl cations and the McLafferty rearrangement (γ-H transfers to O, loss of a neutral alkene), as in butyrophenone (m/z 105 and 120).
sections.learner_can_do: Predict the m/z values of α-cleavage, dehydration, and McLafferty fragments, use the nitrogen rule, and recognize Cl/Br isotope patterns.
sections.game_hook: Each functional group breaks in a signature way; matching the debris pattern to the group unlocks the next clue.

sections.summary: Biological samples use soft ionization—electrospray ionization (ESI) or matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI)—to make protonated ions (M + Hn)n+ with little fragmentation, analyzed by time-of-flight (TOF): ions get the same kinetic energy, so lighter ones fly faster down a drift tube. TOF handles proteins up to ~100 kDa with 3 ppm accuracy (lysozyme 14,306.7578 Da).
sections.learner_can_do: Explain why soft ionization and TOF are used for biomolecules and how flight time relates to mass.
sections.game_hook: A drag race where every ion gets the same push; the finish order reveals their masses.

sections.title: Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum
sections.summary: IR, UV, and NMR are nondestructive and use electromagnetic radiation, a spectrum running from radio waves to gamma rays. Radiation has wavelength λ, frequency ν (Hz), and amplitude; λν = c. Energy comes in photons with ε = hν = hc/λ, so high frequency/short wavelength means high energy. An absorption spectrum records which wavelengths a sample absorbs (IR energy makes bonds stretch and bend; UV promotes electrons).
sections.learner_can_do: Compare and calculate the energies of different kinds of radiation from wavelength or frequency.
sections.game_hook: A light dial from radio to gamma: shorter waves hit harder, and only matching energies get absorbed.

sections.title: Infrared Spectroscopy
sections.summary: Organic chemists use mid-IR from 2.5 to 25 μm, expressed as wavenumbers 4000–400 cm−1 (48.0–4.80 kJ/mol). Bonds vibrate (stretch, bend, wag) at quantized frequencies like atoms joined by springs, and absorb IR radiation when its frequency matches a vibration, increasing the vibration's amplitude. Measuring which frequencies are absorbed reveals which bonds are present.
sections.learner_can_do: Convert between wavelength and wavenumber and explain why molecules absorb only specific IR frequencies.
sections.game_hook: Bonds as springs that only start vibrating harder when you hit their exact resonant frequency.

sections.title: Interpreting Infrared Spectra
sections.summary: IR spectra are complex fingerprints (the 1500–400 cm−1 fingerprint region), but functional groups have characteristic bands (Table 12.1): C=O 1670–1780, O–H 3400–3650 (broad), C=C 1640–1680, ≡C–H 3300, C≡C 2100–2260, C≡N 2210–2260, and so on. The spectrum divides into four regions: 4000–2500 (N–H, C–H, O–H), 2500–2000 (triple bonds), 2000–1500 (double bonds), and below 1500 (fingerprint). Short, strong bonds and bonds to light H vibrate at higher frequency. Hexane, 1-hexene, and 1-hexyne are distinguished by their C=C and C≡C bands.
sections.learner_can_do: Assign functional groups from IR absorption positions and use IR to distinguish isomers (e.g., acetone vs. 2-propen-1-ol).
sections.game_hook: Four IR 'zones' on a spectrum map; a peak landing in a zone lights up the bond type that made it.

sections.title: Infrared Spectra of Some Common Functional Groups
sections.summary: Absent bands are informative too. Alkanes: C–H 2850–2960 and C–C 800–1300 cm−1. Alkenes: =C–H 3020–3100, C=C ~1650, and out-of-plane bends (700–1000) that reveal substitution (monosubstituted 910 and 990, 1,1-disubstituted 890). Alkynes: C≡C 2100–2260 (stronger when terminal) and sharp ≡C–H 3300. Aromatics: C–H 3030, weak 1660–2000, medium 1450–1600, and substitution-revealing bends. Alcohols: broad, intense O–H 3400–3650 (hydrogen bonding). Amines: sharper N–H 3300–3500, two bands for primary, one for secondary. Carbonyls: aldehydes 1730 (1705 conjugated) plus C–H 2750/2850; ketones 1715, with ring strain raising five-membered to 1750 and four-membered to 1780; esters 1735 (1715 conjugated) plus C–O 1000–1300.
sections.learner_can_do: Predict the IR absorptions of a given structure and identify the functional groups of an unknown from its IR spectrum, including the type of carbonyl.
sections.game_hook: An IR scanner whose peaks reveal hidden groups: a broad O–H 'smear', a sharp ≡C–H spike, or a C=O 'tower' whose exact position tells aldehyde from ketone from ester.

back_matter.summary: How to name compounds with several functional groups. A name has four parts—suffix, parent, prefixes, locants. Only one suffix is allowed (except -ene/-yne), chosen by functional-group priority (Table A2: carboxylic acids > anhydrides > esters > thioesters > acid halides > amides > nitriles > aldehydes > ketones > alcohols/phenols > thiols > amines > imines > ethers > sulfides > alkenes/alkynes > alkanes; halides, nitro, and azido are prefix-only). The parent is the longest chain or ring holding the top group; prefixes are alphabetized; parentheses mark complex substituents.
back_matter.learner_can_do: Pick the principal functional group, parent chain, and prefixes to name a polyfunctional compound (e.g., methyl 4-oxopentanoate, 5-amino-2-pentanol).
back_matter.game_hook: A naming tournament where functional groups compete for the suffix slot by priority, and losers become prefixes.
